messages.author: 4d71c6e24fb21497
messages.subject: New integration method and geomorph
parts:
Colleagues,

 

We wish to alert you to a new statistical method for comparing the strength of integration across morphological datasets. The method is based on PLS, and may be used to evaluate whether the degree of integration among partitions is greater in one dataset relative to another. An early view of the paper may be found at:

 

Adams, D.C., and M.L. Collyer. 2016. On the comparison of the strength of morphological integration across morphometric datasets. Evolution.  Accepted. DOI: 10.1111/evo.13045

http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/evo.13045/full  

 

Additionally, version 3.0.3 of geomorph is now available, which includes the new method in a function called ‘compare.pls’. Geomorph 3.0.3 may be installed from CRAN or from the stable branch of geomorph’s github page.

Regards,

Dean and the geomorph team

 

Dr. Dean C. Adams

Professor

Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology

       Department of Statistics

Iowa State University

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] New integration method and geomorph
parts:
Eudald,

I hope you do not mind but I am sharing my reply to our latest email thread with the geomorph R package list, as the conceptual implications might be of interest to others.

In your integration analyses, you have two approaches: one in which you have two modules and another in which you split one of those modules into two separate modules, thus creating three modules.  To your surprise, but exactly as Dean and I posited below, you had instances where impressive integration with two modules was rendered unimpressive with three (and a few cases where the integration increased when going from 2 to 3 modules).  (For reference, I just compared overall Z scores.)  I’ll try to explain how this happens with one hypothetical example.

If you have two modules and high integration, it does not mean that all Procrustes residuals in one module are correlated with all Procrustes residuals in another module.  It means that at least some are more highly correlated than you would expect by chance with random assortment of landmarks into two modules.  If, by chance or by design, you remove a couple of landmarks from one module and these just happen to be the ones that were highly correlated with some in the other module, now the integration between the first two modules, based on (the Procrustes residuals for) remaining landmarks, is greatly reduced.  It is possible that the third module created is still highly integrated with the second one, but the overall integration is averaged for module comparisons 1-2, 2-3, and 1-3, meaning the overall effect could be greatly reduced.  What one can glean from such an outcome is that the landmarks that were switched from the first module to the third module were probably quite integrated with the second module.

In such instances, it might be wise to do as you proposed: run separate analyses on modules 1-2, 2-3, and 1-3 to ascertain for which groups and in which comparison integration is larger or smaller.  There is nothing wrong with this.  In fact, in my opinion, I would argue that this might make more sense than summarizing integration among all modules as the average of integrations between modules.  (Note, the mean is just one way to summarize this.  One could look at the variance, as well.  Or some other summary measure.  The point is that this is what a single statistic is: a summary.)

Here’s maybe another way to think about this problem.  If one performa a Procrustes ANOVA and determines that there is significant shape variation among groups, is this interesting as a final result?  The answer is probably “No”; rather it is an indication that a test of pairwise means is in order.  What you have discovered in your quest is that it is probably prudent to analyses pairwise modular integrations across pairwise group comparisons.  You can address two questions.  Do I see differences in integration in modular comparisons within groups?  Do I see differences among groups for specific modular comparisons?

Either way, you can use comapre.pls to actually address these questions with hypothesis tests.

Good luck!
Mike

Enviat el: dimarts, 29 de novembre de 2016 19:40:56

Tema: RE: [geomorph-r-package] New integration method and geomorph
 
Ha!  Mike’s email got to you before I could finish typing mine. Just re-summarized below.
 
Eudald,

Remember that for 3+ modules, the r-pls is an average across them. So one might obtain curious results if, say, one hypothesized module is not really a ‘good’ biological module while the other 2 are (recall that the user defines the modules, and our intuition of what constitutes a module could be wrong). In this case, the incorrectly defined module might dilute the integration signal found between the two ‘good’ modules.
 
Regardless, the analytics have no way of knowing whether the biologist defined good or bad modules, and like Mike said, the effect of this is at a conceptual/theoretical level remains as-yet unexplored.

Dean

Cc: Eudald Pujol Buxó <epujo...@gmail.com>; Adams, Dean [EEOBS] <dca...@iastate.edu>
Subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] New integration method and geomorph
 
Eudald,
 
I will not likely be able to look at this today, but with three or more modules, I would not be surprised if one gets strange results.  The reason for this is that the pls-r is averaged over pairwise comparisons between modules (1-2, 1-3, 2-3, ….).   My hunch is that this will tend to reduce differences in integration that could be real.  For example, if species 1 has great integration between modules 1-2 and little between 2-3, and species 2 has moderate integration between modules 1-2 and 2-3, the average r values might be similar, and one might miss that species 1 has higher levels of integration, at least in part.
 
I’m not sure if this is what you are getting at.  Regardless, the compare.pls function uses the standard deviation of each test’s random pls-r output to calculate statistics.  It does not distinguish if 2, 3, or more modules are used.  The distributions are what they are.  I might agree if one asserts that the distributions for 3+ modules are misleading, as they are distributions of means rather than specific outcomes, but that is a whole different and yet unexplored area of research.
 
Cheers!
Mike
 
On Nov 29, 2016, at 12:59 PM, eudald pujol buxó <eud...@hotmail.com> wrote:
 
Hi Mike,
 
I have some trouble with the results of the three-module test. I hope I am not bothering you unnecessarily, but the results of the three-module test are somewhat strange, maybe something is wrong or maybe (hopefully) I'm simply wrong myself.
 
I attach here the same dataset with two-module and three-module possibilities of partition, and a script which I tried to make as short and simple to understand as I could. You can simply run the full script and you'll get two panels of plots, one for the two module-analysis and another one for the three-module analysis. 
 
The intriguing thing is that in the three module analysis, the easy-to-understand relationship among "manually" calculated pairwise distances among each sample Zs and the pairwise pvalues or zs disappears. Thus, the only relationship standing in the three-module analysis is the pairwise zs with pairwise pvalues.
 
I read the article in Evolution and I didn't manage to know if this is really a problem of the results. 
Anyway, from the user point of view, it means that when you find significant differences and you make a simple plot(sample.z ~ treat) you find "very distant" samples with non-significant pvalues, while samples having very similar zs get very significant p values.  
 
Well, I hope that at least this helps for future versions of the function if in the end it's simply a normal result.
 
Thanks in advance
 
Eudald

Yes, once fully understood, I tried to make integration tests on pairs of modules and results of the comparisons across groups are much more easy to understand, and even in the end to summarize and explain biologically. For example, in my case it seems that pairwise integration patterns follow very similar tendencies on both species of tadpoles I am working with (probably not a coincidence!).


Thanks very much for this mailing, it's a good way to learn not only how to use a R package but to understand the real calculations and statistics behind it.


Cheers!


Eudald
